Income was clustered: India about 1,200, China 1,060, South Korea 1,550 international dollars. But schooling, health, and fertility already differed markedly. Mean years of schooling ranged from 1 in India to 4 in Korea; life expectancy spanned 33 in China to 54 in Korea; under-five mortality was 241 in India versus 113 in Korea. Fertility was high in India and Korea but lower in China. Over time, Korea’s lines on all panels steepened upward (or downward for mortality and fertility), while India’s crept. The chart argues that countries begin their growth journeys with very different endowments of human capital, and those initial conditions fan out into wider income gaps, not the other way around.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It upends the assumption that low-income countries in 1960 were alike in fundamentals, showing that India’s human-capital deficit was already large.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each panel tracks one measure for all three countries from 1960 onward, but each has its own vertical scale to highlight each country’s trajectory. Compare slopes and starting points, not absolute heights across panels.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not treat the 1960 incomes as identical; they were in the same poor band but not equal, and cross-panel comparisons of heights are meaningless because each panel uses its own scale.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On small screens, the grid stacks into a single column; scroll to see each measure’s story for India, China, and Korea.

chartExplainers.visualId: How long people live
chartExplainers.title: How long people live
chartExplainers.takeaway: Indians today live about 72 years on average, a decade less than South Koreans and six years less than Chinese.
chartExplainers.detail: In the earliest data, India’s life expectancy was about 46 years, above China at 33 but below South Korea at 54 and Vietnam at 58. By the latest measurement, India reached 72 years, while China rose to 78, South Korea to 84, and Vietnam to 75. China’s rapid catch‑up and South Korea’s climb to near the global top reflect early and sustained investments in sanitation, nutrition, and primary care. India’s improvement has been steady but slower, leaving a persistent gap that predated the income divergence. A longer life is both a measure of wellbeing and a prerequisite for accumulating skills and savings.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It shows that East Asia invested in survival first, creating a healthy population as a foundation for later economic growth.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Lines rise over time; steeper slopes mean faster gains in life years.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not assume life expectancy moves in lockstep with current GDP; it reflects decades of health system building.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Observe India’s line rising less steeply than China’s and South Korea’s.

chartExplainers.visualId: Children who don't reach five
chartExplainers.title: Children who don’t reach five
chartExplainers.takeaway: India now loses about 27 children per 1,000 live births before age five, five times higher than China and ten times higher than South Korea.
chartExplainers.detail: At the earliest recorded point, India’s under‑five mortality stood at 241 per 1,000 live births, far worse than China’s 118, South Korea’s 113, or Vietnam’s 99. By the latest figures, India reduced it to 27, but China brought it down to just 6, South Korea to 3, and Vietnam to 17. The steep drops elsewhere came from systematic vaccination, oral rehydration, and maternal health programs rolled out in the 1960s and 1970s. India’s improvement has been substantial but slower, leaving a gap that signals a less robust start for many children. Surviving infancy is the first step in building a productive future workforce.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It captures the earliest and most foundational investment in human capital: whether a child lives to see school age.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Lower is better; the metric is deaths per 1,000 live births, and a sharp decline indicates rapid health improvement.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read this as purely a health outcome; it is an economic indicator of future labour quality and a measure of how a society treats its most vulnerable.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The vertical scale shows India’s decline is impressive but still trailing its peers.

chartExplainers.visualId: Years of schooling, the long view
chartExplainers.title: Years of schooling, the long view
chartExplainers.takeaway: India's average adult has 7.8 years of schooling, a human-capital stock that South Korea had already surpassed by the early 1990s.
chartExplainers.detail: The chart traces the average years of schooling for the adult population from the late 19th century to today. In 1900, India had just 0.16 years, almost identical to China (0.02) and Taiwan (0.02), while South Korea was slightly ahead at 0.3 years. By the latest data, South Korea reaches 13.68 years, Taiwan 12.76, and China 8.99, but India only 7.8. India's climb was slow and steady, adding years after independence, while South Korea's curve steepened dramatically from the 1960s. This gap reflects the speed and scale of public investment in mass schooling: East Asia built universal education early, while India tolerated high out-of-school rates for decades. As a result, India's workforce entered the era of globalized manufacturing with far less formal education, limiting its ability to adopt sophisticated technology.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It answers the foundational question: how much human capital did these countries start with, and how fast did they build it? This chart shows India's educational deficit was cumulative, not just recent.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Vertical axis shows mean years of schooling; horizontal axis is time from 1870 to recent. Each line represents a country. Steep upward slopes indicate rapid educational expansion.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't assume that more years of schooling automatically meant better learning, this chart only shows quantity, not quality.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On a small screen, note India's line stays low while South Korea and Taiwan shoot upward.

chartExplainers.visualId: Years went up; did learning?
chartExplainers.title: Years went up; did learning?
chartExplainers.takeaway: India's learning score sits at 399 on a scale where 625 is advanced, roughly 120 points below Vietnam and South Korea, a gap that means millions of students lack even basic skills.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart shows harmonized test scores, placing different assessments on a common scale capped at 625 for advanced performance. India's score has risen from 355 to 399, while Vietnam scores 519.1 and South Korea 537.21. China scores 441, still above India. These numbers translate into real skill differences: Vietnamese and Korean students can interpret complex texts and solve multistep problems, whereas the typical Indian student often struggles with foundational tasks. The gap has persisted for decades, with East Asian scores actually slightly declining from earlier peaks (South Korea's earlier score was 559.37) but remaining far above India's trajectory. India's relatively stagnant learning outcomes despite rising enrollment suggest that schooling expansion was not paired with quality: poorly trained teachers, rote curricula, and weak accountability systems failed to turn time in class into productive knowledge.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This directly confronts the quality-quantity trade-off: more years of schooling did not guarantee more learning for India. It shows that East Asia built human capital that was both extensive and deep.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Bars represent the latest test score on a common scale of 0–625, where 625 means advanced. Compare bar heights: a higher bar means students learned more per year of schooling.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not misread the slight upward tick in India's score as success, it's still far below peers, and even East Asia's earlier scores were much higher, indicating India's deep learning deficit.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, focus on the stark height difference between India's short bar and Vietnam's and South Korea's tall bars.

chartExplainers.visualId: Where are the women at work?
chartExplainers.title: Where are the women at work?
chartExplainers.takeaway: Only about 32% of working-age women in India are in the labor force, roughly half the share in China, South Korea, and Vietnam.
chartExplainers.detail: The chart traces female labor force participation rates, the share of women aged 15 and older who are working or looking for work, from the 1990s to today. India's rate has barely moved, from 30.3% to 32.4%, while China's hovers around 59.1%, South Korea's is 56.8%, and Vietnam's is 68.6%. East Asia's high participation was sustained by labor-intensive export manufacturing that deliberately drew women into factories, while India's economy created few such jobs. Even more, Indian social norms and safety concerns keep many women out of the paid workforce, and a large share work in unpaid, uncounted household tasks. This gender gap means India effectively wasted half its potential labor supply at a time when East Asian economies were doubling their productive workforce, a critical advantage in their growth spurts.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This chart highlights a glaring demographic outlier: India's missing women in the workforce meant it couldn't harness the full population for industrial output, compounding its educational shortfall.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Lines show the percentage over time. Higher lines mean more women are economically active. Notice India's line hugging the bottom while others stay high, though some decline from early peaks.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't conclude that these numbers fully capture women's work, much of India's female labor is informal or unpaid and undercounted, but even adjusted estimates show a large gap.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On a small screen, watch how India's line barely rises while China, Vietnam, and South Korea all remain above 55%.

chartExplainers.visualId: How fast families shrank
chartExplainers.title: How fast families shrank
chartExplainers.takeaway: India’s fertility dropped from nearly 6 births per woman to about 2 today, but East Asia’s decline was faster and deeper, South Korea now has just 0.75 births per woman.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart plots total fertility rate over time, showing how many children a woman would have during her lifetime. All countries started with high fertility in the 1950s: India had 5.92, South Korea 5.99, Vietnam 6.27, and China 4.45. India's rate slid to 1.96 by 2020, a slow decline, while South Korea's plummeted to 0.75, China's to 1.01, and Vietnam's to 1.9. The pace matters for the dependency ratio: South Korea and China saw fertility halve quickly from the 1970s, meaning each working-age adult supported fewer children sooner, freeing income for savings and investment in education per child. India's gradual decline kept the youth dependency high longer, straining budgets and deferring the demographic sweet spot. Now, India has a chance to capitalize on its still-large working-age population, but fertility is falling fast and the window is narrowing.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It explains why East Asia got a demographic dividend earlier: swift fertility decline reduced the child dependency burden, allowing more investment per child and more women to work. India's slower fertility transition delayed these gains.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Lines show births per woman over time. Steep drops signal a rapid fertility transition. Compare the slope: India's line descends gently, while South Korea's and China's lines plunge.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t interpret low fertility as purely positive, it brings aging challenges, but during their growth phases, East Asia’s rapid declines aided savings, investment, and female labor supply.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, observe that India’s line declines gradually, while South Korea’s line drops steeply to the bottom.

chartExplainers.visualId: Children too short for their age
chartExplainers.title: Children too short for their age
chartExplainers.takeaway: Over a third of Indian children under five are stunted, seven times the rate in China.
chartExplainers.detail: The chart shows the share of children under five who are too short for their age, a measure of chronic malnutrition called stunting. India’s rate fell from an alarming 62.7% in the earliest survey to 35.5% in the latest, a big improvement but still among the highest in the world. China started higher than India’s current level at 38.3% yet brought it down to just 4.8%, while Vietnam dropped from 61.3% to 18.2% and Bangladesh from 70.9% to 23.6%. This is not just about poverty: Vietnam and Bangladesh were poorer than India when they made faster progress. Stunting impairs brain development and lifetime earning potential, so India’s high rate, even after decades of growth, means millions of children are entering adulthood at a permanent disadvantage. The gap between India and its peers reveals a deeper failure in nutrition, sanitation, and maternal health that income gains alone have not fixed.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It translates abstract economic divergence into a bleak human metric: the bodies and brains of the next generation.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each country typically shows two bars: the earliest available survey (darker) and the latest (lighter), representing the percentage of under-fives who are stunted.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not assume these differences simply mirror GDP per person; Bangladesh and Vietnam cut stunting faster from lower income levels, showing that policy and public health systems matter enormously.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: India’s latest stunting rate is 35.5%, versus China’s 4.8% and Vietnam’s 18.2%.

chartExplainers.visualId: How much each country built
chartExplainers.title: How much each country built
chartExplainers.takeaway: China has consistently invested near 40% of its GDP, while India crossed 30% only recently.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart tracks gross fixed capital formation, the share of GDP spent on factories, machinery, roads, and other productive assets, over time. India began at a low 14.5% and gradually climbed to 29.9%, but the journey was slow and uneven. China, by contrast, was already investing 32.6% of GDP in its earliest year shown and pushed that to 39.9%, pouring a staggering share of output into building future capacity. South Korea started even lower, at 11.2%, but then soared to 30% during its industrial miracle, while Vietnam moved from 25.4% to 29%. The persistent gap in the first few decades meant East Asian economies built up a massive stock of infrastructure and manufacturing plants that India lacked, pulling in more technology and creating jobs for millions. Higher investment was not just about quantity; it was also about directing it toward export-oriented industries that could compete globally.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It reveals the raw horsepower behind the East Asian growth engine, a sustained, high level of commitment to building tomorrow’s productive base, which India matched only much later.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each line represents a country’s annual investment rate as a percentage of GDP, plotted from the earliest available data point to the latest.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not conclude that India’s recent 29.9% investment rate means it has caught up; the stock of capital accumulated over decades of lower investment still leaves a wide gap in factories, ports, and roads per worker.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: India’s investment rate rose from 14.5% to 29.9%, but China’s stayed above 32% since the 1980s.

chartExplainers.visualId: Who saved to pay for it
chartExplainers.title: Who saved to pay for it
chartExplainers.takeaway: China’s savings rate of nearly 43% far exceeds the world average of 26%, providing the fuel for massive investment.
chartExplainers.detail: The chart displays gross domestic savings as a share of GDP, showing how much national income is set aside rather than consumed. China’s savings rate started at 33.7% and rose to an extraordinary 42.8%, far above the global average, which crept from 22.9% to just 26.2%. South Korea lifted its savings from 25.8% to 35%, and Vietnam from 21.2% to 36.7%, both nearly doubling the world average. These high savings rates meant that East Asian economies could finance their investment booms largely from domestic resources, avoiding the dangerous reliance on foreign debt that has tripped up other developing nations. The world average barely budged, underlining how exceptional this savings drive was and how it created a virtuous cycle: investment boosted incomes, which allowed more saving, which funded more investment. For India, whose savings rate is not shown here, the implication is stark: without a comparable rise in domestic saving, high investment would have required more foreign borrowing and brought greater risk.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It answers the natural follow‐up: if investment was so high, who paid for it? The answer is mostly domestic thrift, not foreign lenders.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Lines trace the share of GDP saved each year, with the world average providing a baseline; note that all three East Asian nations pull steeply away from the world line.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not interpret high savings as forced austerity or misery; in these cases, it often reflected fast-rising incomes and a conscious strategy to build national capacity, with consumption still growing but at a slower pace than GDP.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: China saves 42.8% of its income, while the world average is 26.2%.

chartExplainers.visualId: Foreign money coming in
chartExplainers.title: Foreign money coming in
chartExplainers.takeaway: Vietnam pulls in FDI worth over 4% of its GDP, while India and China both attract less than 1%.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart shows net inflows of foreign direct investment as a percentage of GDP, a measure of how much foreign capital is being used to build or buy productive assets. India’s inflows started at a negligible 0.1% and have crept up to only 0.7%, despite liberalization. China, interestingly, recorded 0% in its earliest year and just 0.1% in the latest, reflecting its shift from a recipient of FDI to being largely self-financed and even a net outward investor. South Korea remained steady at 0.7% in both periods. Vietnam is the striking outlier: from near zero, it surged to 4.2% of GDP, using foreign factories and technology to drive its manufacturing export boom. For a country at India’s stage, the low FDI numbers suggest missed opportunities to integrate into global production chains, import know-how, and create millions of formal jobs. Vietnam’s success shows how a small economy can punch above its weight by welcoming export-oriented FDI, while India’s larger and more complex market has struggled to attract similar levels relative to its size.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It illustrates how opening to global manufacturing investment gave latecomers a powerful launchpad, a path India largely bypassed.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Bars compare the earliest and latest available years of net FDI inflows as a share of GDP; note that China’s and South Korea’s values are low, while Vietnam’s latest bar dwarfs the others.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not conclude that high FDI is the only route to growth, China’s takeoff relied more on domestic savings, but for countries seeking to industrialize quickly, FDI often brings vital technology and market access that domestic firms lack.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Vietnam attracts FDI worth 4.2% of GDP, over five times India’s 0.7%.

chartExplainers.visualId: How deep the banks went
chartExplainers.title: How deep the banks went
chartExplainers.takeaway: India’s private credit reached just 40% of GDP, while China’s surged to over 194%.
chartExplainers.detail: In the 1960s, India’s domestic credit to the private sector was a tiny 7.8% of GDP, close to South Korea’s 5.7% and Vietnam’s 13.7%. Over the next decades, as East Asian economies industrialised, their financial systems deepened dramatically: South Korea’s credit ratio soared above 160%, China’s to more than 194%, and Vietnam’s to 125%. India’s credit ratio grew far more slowly, reaching only 40%. This shallow financial depth meant businesses had limited access to formal funding for expansion. The gap is partly explained by government-directed lending, high reserve requirements, and a banking sector that long avoided risk.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It sets the foundation for the investment gap: without deep bank lending, firms couldn’t finance the factories and machines that drove East Asia’s growth.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each line is domestic credit to the private sector as a percentage of GDP; a steeper climb means faster financial deepening.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t equate deeper credit with purely market-driven success; China’s and Vietnam’s expansions were heavily state-guided.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Tap lines for exact values; note the huge y-axis gap.

chartExplainers.visualId: What each worker has to work with
chartExplainers.title: What each worker has to work with
chartExplainers.takeaway: An Indian worker has roughly $70,000 in capital to work with, less than a fifth of a South Korean worker’s nearly $400,000.
chartExplainers.detail: In the earliest data, Indian workers had about $6,200 worth of capital stock per worker, compared to $30,200 in South Korea and $9,600 in Taiwan. China began even lower at $2,300. By 2019, India’s capital stock per worker had risen to $68,500, but South Korea’s had ballooned to almost $397,000 and Taiwan’s to over $325,000. Even China, starting from a deeper deficit, accumulated $124,500 per worker. These vast gaps reflect decades of sustained higher investment in physical capital. A worker with more and better machinery is typically more productive, and this shortfall helps explain India’s lower output per person. The data is modelled, so focus on the trajectory rather than exact figures.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This translates the abstract investment rates into a concrete, worker-level measure of the tools available for productivity.
chartExplainers.howToRead: The y-axis is 2017 US dollars per worker; look at how flat India’s line is compared to the steep climbs of the East Asian economies.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t assume this is the sole reason for low output; skills, technology, and infrastructure matter too.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Scrolling vertically shows the massive divergence; rotate for wider view.

chartExplainers.visualId: The factory escalator India never rode
chartExplainers.title: The factory escalator India never rode
chartExplainers.takeaway: India’s manufacturing share shrank from nearly 15% to under 13%, while South Korea’s climbed from 11% to over 26%.
chartExplainers.detail: In the 1960s, Malaysia, Thailand, South Korea, and India all had manufacturing between 10% and 15% of GDP. Over the next half-century, Korea’s factory sector surged to a peak of 29% in 1988 and has stayed above 26%; Malaysia reached over 30% before settling at 22.5%; Thailand hit 28% and now stands at 24.3%. India’s manufacturing, by contrast, never broke past 18% and has since declined to 12.6%, below its starting point. This reflects a pattern of premature deindustrialisation, where services grew faster than manufacturing even at low income levels. The chart excludes China due to data gaps, but its industrial ascent is even more dramatic.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It directly visualizes the missing step in India’s development ladder: the mass factory employment that raised living standards across East Asia.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each line shows manufacturing value added as a share of GDP over time; a hump that stays high signals successful industrialisation.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t think India didn’t industrialise at all; factory output grew in absolute terms, but the economy shifted toward services even faster.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Look for the flat line at the bottom: that’s India, while others rise and plateau.

chartExplainers.visualId: India's leap from farm to office
chartExplainers.title: India's leap from farm to office
chartExplainers.takeaway: Agriculture plunged from 42% to just 16% of GDP, but the share of manufacturing barely moved, while services jumped to half the economy.
chartExplainers.detail: In the early 1960s, agriculture dominated at 41.7% of India’s economy, with services at 38.8%, industry at 20.8%, and manufacturing a modest 14.8%. By the latest data, agriculture had shrunk to 16.3%, but the freed-up share went overwhelmingly to services, which now account for 49.9%. Industry as a whole inched up to 24.6%, but manufacturing within that slipped to 12.6%. This ‘leapfrog’ pattern shows workers moving from farms into informal urban services rather than factory floors. It’s a structural transformation without the middle-income manufacturing boom that filled East Asia’s middle class.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This chart answers ‘where did the output go?’ after agriculture’s decline, revealing the near-total absorption by services.
chartExplainers.howToRead: The lines represent the percentage of GDP from each sector over time; watch how the green services line crosses and overshadows the others.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t conclude that industry was stagnant in absolute terms, it grew, but services grew far faster, shrinking industry’s relative size.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The services line soars; on a small screen, focus on the gap between the 1960 and latest values.

chartExplainers.visualId: Who left the farm, and when
chartExplainers.title: Who left the farm, and when
chartExplainers.takeaway: While South Korea moved over 95% of its workers off the farm, India still has more than two in five workers in agriculture.
chartExplainers.detail: The chart shows the share of employment in agriculture from the early 1990s to the present. India’s agricultural workforce shrank from 63.1% to 41.6%, a decline but leaving a huge fraction still farming. China moved faster, from 59.6% to 21.7%, while Vietnam transformed from 74% to 25%. South Korea, already low at 15.5%, fell further to 5.1%. This slow shift meant India’s economy generated too few productive factory or service jobs to absorb its masses. Stuck in low-yield agriculture, millions remained poor even as GDP grew. The chart captures the very essence of structural transformation, and India’s lag is stark.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This chart directly shows the pace of structural transformation, the very mechanism by which countries get rich, and India’s glacial speed.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Lines show the percentage of total employment in agriculture. Steeper declines mean faster movement into factories and services.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t conclude that farming is bad; the problem is not the farm, but the lack of better-paying alternatives off the farm.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, tap the legend to highlight a single country’s journey.

chartExplainers.visualId: The kind of work India made: informal
chartExplainers.title: The kind of work India made: informal
chartExplainers.takeaway: Nearly nine in ten Indian workers, 87.2%, are informal, without a contract, paid leave, or social security.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart tracks the informal employment rate over time for India, Bangladesh, Indonesia, and Vietnam. India’s informality barely budged: from 90.5% to 87.2%. Bangladesh and Indonesia saw similar stickiness (86.4% to 84% and 85.5% to 81%). Vietnam stands out, cutting its rate from 81.9% to 67%, reflecting its success in creating formal factory jobs. India’s stubbornly high number means the vast majority of work is in tiny, unregistered, low-productivity enterprises. Even during high GDP growth, formal sector employment expanded far too little. This is the missing middle: the route out of poverty through a proper wage-paying job remained blocked for most.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It distinguishes India’s job creation quality: not just how many left the farm, but whether they landed in formal work or informal precarity.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Lines show the percentage of all jobs that are informal. A flat line near the top means informality is entrenched.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t think these workers are ‘unemployed’; they work, but without the protections that formal contracts bring.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Swipe left/right to compare country trajectories.

chartExplainers.visualId: The tariff wall India kept up
chartExplainers.title: The tariff wall India kept up
chartExplainers.takeaway: Even after slashing tariffs from about 81% to under 10%, India’s import duties remain nearly double those of China, South Korea, and Vietnam.
chartExplainers.detail: The chart compares simple average effectively applied tariffs from the late 1980s onward. India’s tariffs plunged from an extreme 80.9%, a legacy of its protectionist era, to 9.8%, yet this is still higher than China (5.4%), South Korea (5.8%), and Vietnam (3.4%). Peer countries started much lower and opened earlier: China was at 39.7% in its early reform days, South Korea was already down to 18.8%. High tariffs kept imported machinery and components expensive, discouraging the export-led manufacturing that drove East Asia’s miracle. Even after liberalization, the wall remained high enough to hinder integration into global value chains. The chart is a blunt measure of an inward-looking strategy that contrasted sharply with the region’s outward orientation.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It captures the policy choice that most powerfully separated India from the export miracle: India chose to shield its home market, while others embraced open trade.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Lines show the simple average tariff on all products. The gap between countries indicates how much higher India’s trade barriers remain.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t ignore that even at 10%, India’s tariffs remain high by global standards, and non-tariff barriers add further costs.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On a small screen, note that the y-axis is scaled to reveal the gaps.

chartExplainers.visualId: India's wall, and how much it waives
chartExplainers.title: India's wall, and how much it waives
chartExplainers.takeaway: India’s actual tariff paid is 9.8%, but its official commitment to other countries averages 14.9%, meaning it waives about a third of its duties through special deals.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart pits India’s MFN (most-favored-nation) applied tariff against the effectively applied tariff. In the early 1990s, the two were nearly identical: MFN at 84.1%, effective at 80.9%. By the latest year, MFN had fallen to 14.9% while effective stood at 9.8%, a gap of over 5 percentage points. The gap reflects preferential access granted under trade agreements, reducing the real cost for some partners but not all. Yet even the lower effective rate of 9.8% remains higher than the standard rates in China, Korea, or Vietnam shown in the previous chart. The headline openness is thus overstated, but the true wall is still the group’s tallest. This nuanced picture shows India is neither fully closed nor truly open.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It tempers the previous chart: the tariff wall is real but partly porous; yet even the lower, true rate keeps India behind.
chartExplainers.howToRead: The top line is India’s advertised tariff; the bottom line is what importers actually pay. The gap between them is waived duties.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t assume India is secretly open; the lower rate is still higher than peers, and many products face much higher specific tariffs.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Focus on the gap between the two lines; in recent years, the spread widens.

chartExplainers.visualId: Climbing the complexity ladder
chartExplainers.title: Climbing the complexity ladder
chartExplainers.takeaway: India's export complexity rose from about 0.4 to 0.7, while South Korea soared to 1.6 and China reached 1.27, showing who mastered harder-to-imitate products.
chartExplainers.detail: In the earliest data, India's Economic Complexity Index (ECI) was 0.38, behind China's 0.63 and far below South Korea's 1.1, while Vietnam was at a deeply negative -0.97. Over the decades, China's index climbed to 1.27 and South Korea's to 1.6, reflecting their deep push into electronics, machinery, and advanced chemicals. India's ECI rose to 0.71, an improvement but still indicative of a basket heavy in textiles, gems, and primary products. Vietnam, the late starter, surged to 0.67, nearly matching India by embedding itself in global supply chains for electronics and apparel. This ranking-based measure captures how diverse and exclusive a country's exports are; a higher number means the country makes things that few others can make. The gap suggests India added less sophisticated capabilities than East Asian economies, which deliberately built up technical education and manufacturing ecosystems.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This chart answers why India's exports never became the high-value, hard-to-imitate goods that power rapid catch-up growth, unlike its peers.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Higher on the scale means a more diverse set of products that few other countries can make; look at the vertical climb of each line over time.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't mistake a small numerical gain for catch-up; ECI is a relative ranking, so a modest absolute rise can still leave a country far behind global leaders.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: India's export complexity inches up while East Asian peers leap ahead.

chartExplainers.visualId: Making things to sell the world
chartExplainers.title: Making things to sell the world
chartExplainers.takeaway: India's share of manufactured exports reached 67.1%, but that still leaves roughly a third as raw materials, while China hit 91.2% and South Korea 87.3%.
chartExplainers.detail: In the early years, India's manufactures were 43.4% of its goods exports, similar to China's 47.7% and higher than South Korea's mere 18.2%, which was then a largely agricultural exporter. South Korea transformed most dramatically, pushing the share to 87.3%, fueled by aggressive moves into electronics, autos, and steel. China surpassed everyone, hitting 91.2%, as it became the world's factory. Vietnam, from a comparable 44% starting point, now stands at 85%, driven by foreign investment in textiles and electronics assembly. India's rise to 67.1% is progress, but it means about one-third of its goods exports are still commodities like fuels, ores, and agricultural products, limiting value addition and making it vulnerable to global price cycles. The East Asian path shows that sustaining rapid growth typically involves shifting the export engine into manufactures.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This chart lays bare the composition gap: India never built the manufacturing export juggernaut that powered East Asian growth.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Higher bars mean more of a country's goods exports are manufactured items; watch how each country's bar grew from the earliest to latest value.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't assume India's 67.1% suggests a services powerhouse automatically fills the gap; this graph is only about merchandise trade, and services are a separate story.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: India's manufacturing export share lags behind all East Asian comparators shown.

chartExplainers.visualId: Who captured world trade
chartExplainers.title: Who captured world trade
chartExplainers.takeaway: India's share of world goods exports crept from 1.1% to 1.8%, while China exploded from 2.1% to 14.6%, capturing the lion's share of global trade.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart tracks each country's slice of all merchandise exports worldwide. In the earliest data, India stood at 1.1% and China at 2.1%, not dramatically apart. But China's line then climbs relentlessly, reaching 14.6% as it became the workshop of the world, integrating into global supply chains after opening up. South Korea starts at practically zero and climbs to 2.8%, exceeding India's share despite having a much smaller population. Vietnam, starting at a negligible 0.1%, reaches 1.6%, almost level with India. India's share edges up to 1.8%, an increase but still a minor presence in world trade relative to its population and aspirations. This metric reflects not just export growth but competitiveness relative to other exporting nations; to raise your share, you must out-grow the world average. East Asian economies achieved that through export-oriented manufacturing booms; India's slower manufacturing growth kept its share low.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It sums up the asymmetry of global trade: India remained a bit player while Asian peers grabbed disproportionate shares.
chartExplainers.howToRead: The higher the line, the larger the country's claim on all goods exported worldwide; time runs along the bottom.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't think 1.8% versus 14.6% is only about size; India has a huge population, so its per-capita trade performance is even more meager.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: China's world trade share dwarfs India's, which stayed under 2%.

chartExplainers.visualId: Plugged into the world's supply chains
chartExplainers.title: Plugged into the world's supply chains
chartExplainers.takeaway: Vietnam’s exports now are nearly half foreign inputs at 48.5%, while India’s backward GVC participation sits at 25.7%, reflecting far shallower integration into global production networks.
chartExplainers.detail: Backward participation measures how much of a country's exports consist of inputs imported from abroad. India started at 10.6%, lower than Korea's 25.7% and Vietnam's 20.2%, while China was at 13.9%. Over time, Vietnam's share shot up to 48.5%, meaning almost half the value of its exports comes from imported components, a hallmark of its electronics and textile assembly roles. Korea, with its advanced manufacturing, rose to 36.7%, reflecting intricate supply chains for autos and semiconductors. China's participation dipped slightly to 17%, likely due to its growing domestic supply chains and upward shift into higher value-added activities. India's rise to 25.7% shows some deepening, but it remains well below the most integrated economies. This matters because supply-chain integration often brings technology transfer and efficiency gains, and India's lower number hints at manufacturing that relies more on domestic inputs and simpler processes.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It shows India never became a vital node in the world's production chains, while Vietnam plugged in deeply to drive its export surge.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A higher bar means more of a country's exports are made from imported inputs; compare the starting and ending bars for each.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't think a low share is always bad; large economies may naturally source more domestically, but India's number also reflects limited participation in the most dynamic manufacturing networks.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Vietnam's exports are nearly half foreign inputs; India's are only a quarter.

chartExplainers.visualId: Becoming China's customer
chartExplainers.title: Becoming China's customer
chartExplainers.takeaway: India's imports from China exploded from $1.5 billion to nearly $127 billion, while exports inched to just $14.9 billion, creating a yawning deficit.
chartExplainers.detail: A line chart of bilateral trade in current US dollars: imports from China and exports to China. In the earliest year, India imported $1.5 billion and exported $735 million, imports were already double exports. By the latest year, imports had multiplied 85 times to $127 billion, while exports grew to only $14.9 billion. The gap widened from $0.7 billion to over $112 billion. This reflects India’s role as a consumer of Chinese electronics, machinery, and chemicals, while its own exports remain primary goods like iron ore. The deficit shows how India got left out of the manufacturing value chains that other Asian economies joined.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This chart answers why India’s trade relationship with China is lopsided, unlike other Asian nations that became suppliers to China’s factories.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A line chart with two lines of current US dollars over time: the soaring line is imports, the flat line is exports. The growing gap is the trade deficit.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t assume all imports are finished consumer goods; some are components for Indian assembly, but the sheer scale still highlights manufacturing weakness.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The import line rocketing upward while the export line barely moves is a visual punch.

chartExplainers.visualId: How much each worker produces
chartExplainers.title: How much each worker produces
chartExplainers.takeaway: While India’s output per hour rose from $1.9 to $8.1, South Korea’s soared to $53.6, a productivity leap India missed.
chartExplainers.detail: The chart plots output per hour worked in international dollars for India, China, South Korea, and Taiwan. In the earliest year, Taiwan led at $8.3, while India stood at $1.9, China at $0.7, and Korea at $2.8. By the latest year, Korea and Taiwan had raced past $50, China had climbed to $17.7, but India reached only $8.1. India started in the middle of the pack but ended far behind because its productivity growth averaged barely 3% per year versus East Asia’s sustained 5–6%. Without rising output per hour, incomes cannot rise broadly. The East Asian miracle is really a productivity miracle, built on investment, skills, and technology adoption.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This distills the income gap to its root cause: the value created per hour of work, showing India’s growth lacked the productivity revolution seen elsewhere.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A line chart with multiple countries over time; the vertical axis is international dollars per hour. Compare how India’s line rises gently while others arc steeply upward.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t confuse output per hour with wages; this measures total economic value produced per hour, not what workers are paid.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Korea’s line turns nearly vertical; India’s slope is much flatter.

chartExplainers.visualId: Spending on inventing the future
chartExplainers.title: Spending on inventing the future
chartExplainers.takeaway: India’s R&D spending remained frozen at 0.6% of GDP for decades, while South Korea more than doubled to 4.9%, funding an innovation leap.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart tracks research and development expenditure as a share of GDP. India’s line is almost flat at 0.6% from the earliest to latest year, unchanged over decades. South Korea started at 2.1% and then surged to a world-leading 4.9%, China rose from 0.6% to 2.6%, and Japan held steady around 2.6–3.4%. Innovation economies require sustained R&D, Korea now outspends everyone to lead in semiconductors and electronics. India’s static investment means fewer patents, slower technology absorption, and little corporate research outside pharmaceuticals and IT services. This feeds directly into productivity and export sophistication gaps.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It explains why India’s firms haven’t moved up the value chain: without serious R&D, you cannot create the proprietary technologies that drive high-value exports.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A line chart over time, R&D as % of GDP. India’s line is a flat pancake near zero; Korea’s is a steep climb to the top.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t conclude that R&D spending automatically guarantees growth, or that India’s frugal innovation never works; but the scale of the gap is enormous and telling.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: India’s line is nearly horizontal; Korea’s points to the stars.

chartExplainers.visualId: The power to run a factory
chartExplainers.title: The power to run a factory
chartExplainers.takeaway: India’s electricity use per person barely passed 1,180 kWh, while South Korea’s exceeds 11,350 kWh, marking a vast industrial power gap.
chartExplainers.detail: The chart shows electric power consumption per capita in kilowatt-hours. In the earliest year, India used 271 kWh per person, not far behind China’s 511 and well ahead of Vietnam’s 99. By the latest year, China had soared to 6,524, South Korea to 11,350, and Vietnam to 2,585, but India reached only 1,182. Electricity consumption heavily correlates with factory output, cold storage, and modern household appliances. Vietnam, a late industrialiser, now consumes twice as much per person as India. This partly reflects India’s service-led growth path and chronic under‑investment in power generation and grid connectivity, which holds back manufacturing.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It gives a visceral proxy for industrial muscle and broad-based living standards that GDP figures alone can obscure.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A line chart of kWh per person. Watch India’s line rise modestly while all others steeply ascend, with Korea soaring to over 11,000.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t read this as total power output; India generates huge total electricity, but on a per‑person basis it is still very low. Also, some economies with less heavy industry stay lower.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The lines for Korea and China race upward; India’s remains stubbornly flat.

chartExplainers.visualId: Moving to the city
chartExplainers.title: Moving to the city
chartExplainers.takeaway: While 81% of South Koreans live in cities, India's urban share is just over a third.
chartExplainers.detail: In the earliest data, all four countries were between 15% and 28% urban. Since then, China and South Korea have surged to about 66% and 81% urban, while India moved from roughly 18% to just over 35%. This is not simply about bigger cities, it reflects where jobs concentrate. East Asia's factory and export booms pulled millions into dense urban centers, which in turn raised productivity. India's slower pace mirrors its smaller manufacturing footprint and the enduring weight of village livelihoods. Even Vietnam, starting lower, now edges ahead of India, showing that urbanisation follows the pull of productive urban work. The result is that most Indians still live outside the agglomeration that powered other Asian transformations.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Urbanisation is the physical map of economic transformation, and this chart shows India never pulled people into cities at East Asia's pace, which explains where factories and jobs didn't cluster.
chartExplainers.howToRead: The y-axis shows the share of population living in urban areas; lines track each country from their earliest data to the latest.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't assume India's urbanisation rate is similar to China's because they both started low; China's pace was much faster.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On small screens, watch how China and South Korea's lines pull away sharply from India's around the 1980s.

chartExplainers.visualId: The capable state
chartExplainers.title: The capable state
chartExplainers.takeaway: South Korea's government effectiveness ranks in the 80th percentile, but India's hovers near the 59th, limiting its ability to execute grand plans.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart tracks expert ratings of public services, civil service quality, and policy implementation. India began around the 47th percentile and has climbed to the 59th, a genuine improvement, but still middle-of-the-pack. China's line rose much steeper, reaching the top third, while South Korea now sits in the top fifth globally. The gap matters because an effective state can plan infrastructure, staff schools and clinics, and enforce regulations consistently. India's middling rating reflects a bureaucracy where rules are plentiful but delivery lags, slowing the translation of policies into outcomes on the ground. Vietnam, despite its lower starting point, has caught up to India's early level, hinting at its own state-building progress.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: State capacity is the hidden engine behind successful industrial policy and public investment, and this chart reveals India's persistent middle-rank, unlike the top-tier states of East Asia.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each line shows the country's percentile rank among all nations for government effectiveness; higher means more capable. Look at where each line ends.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't read this as India being inept; it's improved, but relative to countries like South Korea, it still lags.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The gap between South Korea's line and India's widens dramatically after 2000.

chartExplainers.visualId: Where India scores, and where it doesn't
chartExplainers.title: Where India scores, and where it doesn't
chartExplainers.takeaway: India's voice and rule of law top the 55th percentile, but its corruption control sinks to just the 42nd, exposing a delivery deficit.
chartExplainers.detail: India's governance is a mixed picture. On the democratic dimensions, voice and accountability, and rule of law, it ranks around the 56th percentile, meaning it does better than about half of countries. But on the delivery side, government effectiveness sits at the 59th and control of corruption drops to just above the 42nd. This pattern matters for development: open politics and legal systems don't automatically build roads, maintain power grids, or stamp out graft. The low corruption score signals that public resources leak and firms face uncertainty, which can deter the sustained investment that powered East Asian growth. It's a reminder that institutional quality is multidimensional, and India's strengths in political freedoms haven't fully translated into the administrative capacity needed for economic transformation.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This explains why India's democratic strengths haven't automatically created an industrial miracle, the chart pinpoints the specific governance weaknesses that matter for economic delivery.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each bar is India's percentile rank among all countries for that governance dimension; the higher the bar, the better India compares globally.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't conflate voice and accountability with effective governance; the chart shows they don't go hand-in-hand in India's case.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Note the drop from rule of law and voice to the shorter bar for corruption control.

chartExplainers.visualId: The growth-rate gap behind the income gap
chartExplainers.title: The growth-rate gap behind the income gap
chartExplainers.takeaway: India's early decades crept at 1.4% a year while South Korea powered ahead at 6.8%, and even recent Indian growth at 4% hasn't closed the gap.
chartExplainers.detail: From the 1960s through the 2010s, the gap in growth rates explains almost the entire income divergence. South Korea sustained 6.8% per capita growth in its early decades, lifting average incomes rapidly. China's growth accelerated to 6% in the latest decade. India, in contrast, managed barely 1.4% a year early on, and even after reforms, averaged 4% in the latest decade. This means an Indian worker's income doubled roughly every 50 years until 1980, while a South Korean's doubled every decade. The compound effect is devastating: even India's recent 4% is only half of what Korea and China sustained for longer. Vietnam's climb from negative growth to nearly 5% mirrors a late-industrialisation story, but it still outpaces India's record.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This chart distills the entire divergence into one visual: it's not that India never grew, but that East Asia grew so much faster for so long that the income gap became vast.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each dot represents a decade's average annual growth in income per person; lines connect the dots to show the trajectory.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't misinterpret South Korea's recent lower growth as failure; it's a sign of an already rich economy where rapid catch-up is over.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On small screens, track India's consistently lower line, especially in the early decades.

chartExplainers.visualId: Sweat or smarts?
chartExplainers.title: Sweat or smarts?
chartExplainers.takeaway: South Korea’s total factor productivity surged from 0.25 to 0.61 of the US frontier, while India crept from 0.35 to just 0.44.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart tracks total factor productivity (TFP) relative to the United States, a measure of how efficiently each economy uses its capital and labor. South Korea and Taiwan both made dramatic leaps; Taiwan reached 0.86 of the US level, the highest of the group, while South Korea tripled its ratio. India’s improvement was far more modest, rising only nine percentage points over the same period. China actually saw its relative efficiency dip slightly from 0.46 to 0.40. These patterns broadly suggest that East Asia’s growth came from smarter use of resources, not just more machines and workers. Because TFP is a residual, the numbers are best read as a general direction rather than precise efficiency scores.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It tests whether Asia’s growth miracle was simply a build-up of inputs or a genuine leap in efficiency, and India’s slow improvement reveals a important gap.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each line shows a country’s TFP as a fraction of the US level (1.0); a rising line means the economy is becoming more efficient relative to the US.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t treat TFP as a pure technology measure; it captures everything not explained by capital and labor, including measurement error.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On a phone, focus on the steep climbs of Korea and Taiwan versus the gentle rise of India.

chartExplainers.visualId: The demographic window, and who used it
chartExplainers.title: The demographic window, and who used it
chartExplainers.takeaway: India’s working-age share climbed from 56% to 68%, but South Korea turned a similar rise into a manufacturing export boom.
chartExplainers.detail: The chart plots the share of the population aged 15 to 64 for India, China, South Korea, and Vietnam. All four started between 54% and 56% in the early years and saw their working-age shares peak near 70%. South Korea reached 70% earliest, while China and Vietnam hit similar levels later. India’s share is still rising at 68% and has not yet peaked. The key insight is not the number itself but what was done with the workers: East Asian countries absorbed their bulges into productive industry, generating a demographic dividend. Without jobs, the same bulge becomes a burden. India’s window remains open, but time is limited to turn potential into prosperity.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It reveals that demographics alone don’t explain the divergence; the important difference was whether countries used the window for mass employment.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each line shows the percentage of the total population that is of working age (15-64); a higher line means a larger potential workforce.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: A rising share does not automatically deliver growth; it is only a dividend if workers find productive work.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Notice how the lines rise together but then plateau at different times and heights, with India still ascending.

chartExplainers.visualId: Did the growth reach everyone?
chartExplainers.title: Did the growth reach everyone?
chartExplainers.takeaway: India’s top 10% now capture nearly 59% of pre-tax national income, up from 38%, a sharper concentration than in China, Korea, or Indonesia.
chartExplainers.detail: This graph shows the share of national income captured by the richest 10% of the population. India’s line is the most striking: it shot upward from 38% to almost 59%, one of the steepest rises among major economies. China started lower, at 28%, and reached about 42%, while South Korea’s share rose only modestly from 32% to 38%. Indonesia fell in between, ending at roughly 47%. These numbers blend survey and tax data, so rankings and trends matter more than precise percentages. Yet the direction is clear: India’s growth has been accompanied by a sharp concentration at the top, unlike the more equalizing paths of early East Asian industrialization.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It separates the story of aggregate growth from how that growth is shared, highlighting that India’s expansion has been exceptionally top-heavy.
chartExplainers.howToRead: A rising line means the richest 10% are taking a larger slice of the pie; a flat line means the distribution is stable.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not conclude that the poor in India got poorer in absolute terms; even with rising inequality, average incomes have risen, though the gains are skewed.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On a small screen, focus on how India’s line breaks away upward from the pack.

chartExplainers.visualId: So when does India catch up?
chartExplainers.title: So when does India catch up?
chartExplainers.takeaway: If India maintains its recent growth pace, it would still need until around 2043 to reach China’s current income of $24,000 per person, and it remains short of South Korea’s $55,000 by mid-century.
chartExplainers.detail: This projection extends India’s GDP per capita forward at the average growth rate it achieved from 2014 to 2024, while holding China and South Korea at their current levels. India starts near $2,200 and, under this simple assumption, climbs to roughly $43,400 by mid-century. China’s flat line sits at about $24,000, a level India reaches roughly two decades from now. South Korea’s line is far higher, near $55,000, well beyond India’s simulated reach even by mid-century. The exercise is purely illustrative, freezing the East Asian countries in place, which of course they will not do. It underscores that even sustained rapid growth requires generations to close enormous income gaps.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It provides a sobering timeline for convergence, answering the reader’s likely final question: how long before India is as rich as its neighbors?
chartExplainers.howToRead: India’s line slopes upward over time; the horizontal lines for China and Korea show their current income levels; where India’s line crosses a horizontal line is the catch-up year under these simple assumptions.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: This is not a forecast; if India’s growth slows, the crossing point moves further out, and in reality China and Korea will continue to advance. And the target itself is moving: China is slowing hard in the 2020s, with a property crash and a shrinking workforce, so freezing it at today's level flatters neither side.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The large gap between India’s projected line and Korea’s flat line is especially dramatic on a phone; scroll to see the long horizon.

chartExplainers.visualId: The poverty India did crush
chartExplainers.title: The poverty India did crush
chartExplainers.takeaway: India slashed its $3-a-day extreme poverty from nearly 60% to about 5%, pulling hundreds of millions out of destitution.
chartExplainers.detail: The chart tracks the share of people living on less than $3 per day (in 2011 PPP terms) for India and select Asian peers from the earliest year available to the latest. India’s rate fell dramatically from 59.7% to just 5.3%, meaning roughly 700 million people escaped extreme poverty. This is a genuine triumph, achieved even without the manufacturing boom that lifted East Asia. However, the trajectory was slower than in China, which crashed from 97% to effectively zero, or Vietnam, which dropped from 57.5% to 1.6%. India’s data points are sparse due to gaps in consumption surveys, so the trend line may smooth over periods of faster or slower progress. The remaining 5.3% still represents tens of millions of people, and the dashed lines between points remind us that the journey isn’t over.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This chart shows India’s most undeniable achievement, a human-scale victory that often gets lost in comparisons of GDP or exports.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each line shows the percentage of a country’s population living below the $3/day extreme poverty line. The vertical axis is the share in poverty (0 to 100%), and the horizontal axis is time.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t look at the final numbers and conclude India has solved poverty; the sparse survey data can mask recent reversals, and $3/day is still a very low bar.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On small screens, focus on India’s steep fall, from roughly 6 in 10 to less than 1 in 20.

chartExplainers.visualId: India's other escalator: services
chartExplainers.title: India's other escalator: services
chartExplainers.takeaway: Services ballooned from 15% to nearly 46% of India’s exports, a route that China, Korea, and even Vietnam barely took.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart shows the services share of total goods and services exports for India and key Asian economies. India’s services share climbed from 15.3% to 45.6%, a near-tripling that reflects its rise as a global IT and business-process outsourcing hub. In contrast, the share for China (10.6% to 10.1%), South Korea (16.3% to 16.8%), and Vietnam (23.6% to 5.8%) remained low or even fell, as these countries concentrated on manufacturing exports. A high services share is not inherently good or bad, but in India’s case, these are high-skill services that employ relatively few low-skilled workers directly. This ‘escalator’ has lifted millions into the middle class but left behind those who would have worked in factories in a more traditional growth path. The chart thus highlights a structural difference: India found a niche, but it hasn’t yet translated into mass employment.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It answers the puzzle: if India is poor at exporting goods, how does it export at all? This reveals the unique service-led escape route.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each line represents the percentage of a country’s total exports (goods plus services) that come from services. The axis runs from 0% to 50%+, and the series cover decades.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read a rising services share as automatically superior; in these comparisons, it signals what India didn’t do, build a broad factory floor.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, watch India’s line rising while others stay flat or fall.

chartExplainers.visualId: The all-in human scorecard
chartExplainers.title: The all-in human scorecard
chartExplainers.takeaway: India’s Human Development Index rose from 0.45 to 0.69, but that still places it behind Vietnam (0.77) and far adrift of China (0.80) and South Korea (0.94).
chartExplainers.detail: The Human Development Index combines life expectancy, education, and income into a single score from 0 to 1. India’s journey from 0.45 to 0.69 represents real gains: people live longer, children stay in school longer, and incomes are higher. Yet the gap with its peers is stark. Viet Nam, starting from 0.5, reached 0.77, and China moved from 0.49 to 0.80. South Korea, already at 0.74 in the earliest data, now basks at 0.94. This broad measure captures India’s weakness across all dimensions simultaneously, it’s not just about GDP. The fact that even Vietnam, with a lower starting point and lower income, overtook India underscores how India’s patchy public health and education systems held back human capability.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It gives the whole picture in one number, showing that India’s growth didn’t translate into human well-being as effectively as in East Asia.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each line plots a country’s HDI score, which runs from 0 (lowest) to 1 (highest), over time. Higher is better.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t assume that India’s HDI is low just because of income; it’s a composite, so health and education shortfalls pull it down too.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On a small screen, the key is the order: Korea on top, then China, Vietnam, and India trailing.

chartExplainers.visualId: The road not taken: democracy
chartExplainers.title: The road not taken: democracy
chartExplainers.takeaway: India’s electoral democracy score rose from a fragile 0.08 to 0.38, even as East Asian tigers like South Korea and Taiwan languished near zero before their eventual leaps.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart uses the V-Dem electoral democracy index, which scores countries from 0 (autocracy) to 1 (full democracy) based on clean elections, freedoms, and checks on power. India started from a low 0.23 at independence (a fragile 0.08 under colonial rule in 1900) but climbed to 0.38, reflecting a messy but persistent democratic journey. Meanwhile, South Korea and Taiwan began at near zero under authoritarian regimes, only spiking to 0.82 and 0.80 after democratization in the 1980s and 1990s. China has barely budged, hovering around 0.07. The chart doesn’t claim that democracy boosts or hinders growth; it simply shows the political context in which India’s development unfolded. The contrast is honest: India’s relatively open society coexisted with slower economic transformation, while East Asia’s rapid industrialization often occurred under repressive rule.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This is the moral counterweight, the chart that explains why India’s path, for all its flaws, offered freedoms that the East Asian miracles didn’t.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Lines track the V-Dem electoral democracy index, from 0 (fully autocratic) to 1 (fully democratic). Steep rises indicate democratic transitions.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don’t use this chart to claim democracy caused India’s slower growth; it only shows the simultaneous trajectories, not a causal link.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, focus on India’s slow rise and South Korea’s dramatic leap.

chartExplainers.visualId: What India's firms say holds them back
chartExplainers.title: The biggest obstacles Indian firms reported in 2014
chartExplainers.takeaway: In 2014, roughly one in five Indian firms named corruption as their single biggest impediment, and another 15% pointed to unreliable electricity, together dwarfing the share that blamed labour regulations (under 4%).
chartExplainers.detail: This World Bank Enterprise Survey asked Indian firms to name the one obstacle most harmful to their operations. Corruption topped the list at about 20% of responses, followed by electricity at roughly 15%. Tax rates and access to finance each troubled 12-13% of firms, while just 3.7% cited labour regulations. The pattern suggests that, a decade ago, the immediate business climate, unpredictable power and red tape, was far more pressing than the labour-law narrative often invoked in reforms. It underscores that the voice of firms can redirect attention toward infrastructure and governance deficits that often escape the headlines.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This chart grounds the growth debate in the words of businesses themselves, challenging the assumption that labour laws were the dominant constraint on Indian manufacturing a decade ago.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each bar represents the share of firms in the 2014 survey that chose that obstacle as their single greatest difficulty; the horizontal axis shows percentages.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read this as current reality, it is a single snapshot from 2014, nor conclude that labour laws are trivial; the survey forced a single choice, so firms might still have faced multiple hurdles.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Tallest bars: corruption and electricity. Labour regulations appear as a short bar near the bottom.

chartExplainers.visualId: The sanitation gap behind the stunting
chartExplainers.title: The sanitation gap behind the stunting
chartExplainers.takeaway: India entered the 2000s with worse sanitation than Bangladesh and only recently caught up, after the cohort now of working age had already been stunted.
chartExplainers.detail: In 2000 only about 15% of Indians used even a basic toilet, against 57% in China and near-universal coverage in Korea and Japan. India has since climbed to roughly 83%, a rapid gain driven by a large state push, but sanitation in the years that matter most for a child's growth was among the worst in the region.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It supplies the explanation the stunting chart leaves open: open defecation in a dense country spreads the disease that stops a child absorbing nutrition, which is why Indian children are shorter than even poorer peers who eat less.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Follow India's line from the bottom in 2000 as it climbs toward the others; the gap in the early years is the part that shaped today's adults.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't read a recently built toilet as undoing past harm; stunting is set early in life and is largely permanent.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Focus on India's line against China and the world; the early gap is the point.

chartExplainers.visualId: Farms that never caught up
chartExplainers.title: Farms that never caught up
chartExplainers.takeaway: India's land yields little more than half what China, Korea or Vietnam now grow per hectare, a gap that opened with land reform and never closed.
chartExplainers.detail: A Korean hectare grew three times as much grain as an Indian one as far back as 1961. India's Green Revolution lifted yields from about 950 to 3,600 kg per hectare, real progress, but China, Korea and Vietnam now harvest around 6,000 and India still trails.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: How Asia Works puts land reform first: redistributing land raised yields, fed the cities and financed the first factories. India's failure to redistribute left a low-yield farm sector that threw off less surplus and freed fewer hands.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each line is kilograms of cereal per hectare; the higher and steeper, the more productive the land became.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't attribute the whole gap to policy; irrigation, crop mix and climate matter too. It is one strand of the story.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Compare India's line with China and Korea; the persistent gap is the takeaway.

chartExplainers.visualId: Did India ever become an exporter?
chartExplainers.title: Did India ever become an exporter?
chartExplainers.takeaway: Vietnam's exports are worth about 90% of GDP and Korea's reached 44%; India's only crept to about 21% and then drifted sideways.
chartExplainers.detail: Cutting tariffs is only half of opening up. The tigers reorganised their economies to sell to the world. India's exports rose from 5% of GDP in 1960 to a peak in the early 2010s before easing back, never becoming the engine they were elsewhere.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Export orientation is the heart of the East Asian model, and this is the cleanest single measure of whether a country actually adopted it. India leaned on its home market instead.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each line is exports as a share of GDP; higher means more export-oriented.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Large economies trade less as a share of GDP than small ones, so part of India's lower ratio is size. Read the trend and the contrast with Vietnam and Korea, not the exact level.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Vietnam's and Korea's lines against India's flat one carry the story.

chartExplainers.visualId: The sophisticated goods India doesn't make
chartExplainers.title: The sophisticated goods India doesn't make
chartExplainers.takeaway: Vietnam went from below India to 44% of its manufactured exports being high-tech; India crept from 10% to 19%.
chartExplainers.detail: The complexity index measures sophistication in the round; this is the blunt version, the share of exports that are electronics, instruments and other high-technology goods. Vietnam's leap came from joining the electronics supply chains of firms like Samsung.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It shows the sophistication gap in concrete products, and shows a latecomer overtaking India fast by climbing onto the assembly rung India has been slow to take.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each line is the high-tech share of a country's manufactured exports.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: The high-tech label tracks the product, not the local value added; much of Vietnam's is assembly of imported parts, so it overstates depth. But assembly is how Korea and China began too.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Watch Vietnam's line cross above India's; that crossover is the point.

chartExplainers.visualId: Selling inputs, not assembling them
chartExplainers.title: Selling inputs, not assembling them
chartExplainers.takeaway: India isn't shut out of supply chains, it's upstream: about 41% of its export value is domestic inputs feeding others' production, above its 26% backward share. Vietnam is the mirror image.
chartExplainers.detail: Forward participation counts the domestic value (raw materials, chemicals, software, design) embedded in intermediate exports that partners finish and re-export. India's runs near 41%, above its 26% backward share; Vietnam's fell from 41% to 25% as its assembly role pushed backward participation past 48%.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It corrects the impression from the backward-participation chart that India is disconnected. India is integrated, just from the upstream, input-supplying side, which generates far fewer factory jobs than downstream assembly.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each line is domestic value added in a country's intermediate exports as a share of gross exports; higher means more of an upstream, input-supplying role.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't read a high forward share as superior; commodity exporters like Indonesia rank highest. Forward and backward are two halves of integration, not a quality ranking.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Compare India's flat-high line with Vietnam's falling one; they crossed as Vietnam became an assembler.

chartExplainers.visualId: The services hidden inside the exports
chartExplainers.title: The services hidden inside the exports
chartExplainers.takeaway: By 2022 about 44% of the value in everything India exported was domestically produced services, the highest in the peer group; Vietnam's assembly model stripped its share to 10%.
chartExplainers.detail: Trade-in-value-added accounting pulls out the design, software, logistics and finance baked into exports, goods included. India's services value-added share rose from 31% in the mid-1990s to 44%, edging above Japan, while Vietnam's fell to about 10%.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It is the deepest version of the article's recurring point: India's advantage runs through services so thoroughly they dominate the value of its goods exports too, which lifts skilled workers more than factory labour.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each line is the share of gross exports made up of domestic services value added; higher means a more services-driven export base.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't confuse this with services sold directly across the border (the previous chart); this is services value embedded inside all exports, goods included.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: India's rising line versus Vietnam's low one carries the contrast.

sourceNotes: Long-run GDP per capita and decade growth rates: Maddison Project Database.
Current international dollar PPP income estimates: IMF World Economic Outlook (April 2025).
Health, demographic, learning, investment, finance, economic structure, trade, electricity and poverty data: World Bank.
Schooling attainment: Lee-Lee and Barro-Lee datasets.

Tariff profiles: WITS; India–China bilateral trade: UN Comtrade; economic complexity: Harvard Growth Lab Atlas of Economic Complexity; productivity, capital per worker and TFP: Penn World Table; value chain participation: OECD TiVA; top income shares: World Inequality Database; human development: UNDP Human Development Index; electoral democracy index: V-Dem.
Worldwide Governance Indicators and the 2014 India Enterprise Survey: World Bank.
caveats: Maddison Project pre-1950 GDP figures are reconstructions and should be read as broad trajectories, not exact levels.
PPP incomes are a modelled price adjustment; the income chart uses current-dollar IMF PPP while the convergence projection uses constant-price World Bank PPP.
Learning scores, governance ranks, and the 2014 Enterprise Survey are snapshots that may not capture long-run trends.

Labour-force informality and some employment figures come from modelled estimates (ILOSTAT) and differ from India's household surveys; comparable informality data for China and Korea are not available from ILOSTAT.
The convergence projection is a simple constant-growth illustration, not a forecast; actual growth will vary.
Several factors moving together in the data does not prove that any single one caused the divergence.

This page measures India mainly against East Asia's successes (South Korea, Taiwan, China, Vietnam), which are the rare winners of the development race, not a baseline every country reaches. Set against its own South Asian neighbourhood, India looks less like a failure than the stronger half of a hard pack.

The manufacturing-export path East Asia rode may be narrowing: automation means factories now hire far fewer workers, so the route this page faults India for missing is contested in current research, and India's tilt toward services may be an early adaptation rather than a simple mistake. What replaces the factory as a mass-employment escalator is genuinely unsettled.

China, the headline success on this page, is itself slowing sharply in the 2020s, with a property crash, deflation and a shrinking workforce, so the convergence comparison freezes a moving and now-wobbling target.
