plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank · life expectancy at birth · 1960 to latest
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: East Asia invested in survival first; the life-expectancy gap opened decades before the income gap.

plannedCharts.title: Children who don't reach five
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank · under-five mortality · 1960 to latest
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: A healthy, surviving child is the first input into a future workforce.

plannedCharts.title: Years of schooling, the long view
plannedCharts.subtitle: Lee-Lee / Barro-Lee via Our World in Data · average years of schooling, adults · the human-capital stock, not just enrolment
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Schooling is the human-capital stock a country brings to industrialisation; India started this climb late and slow.

plannedCharts.title: Years went up; did learning?
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank Human Capital Project · harmonised test scores, latest available · a score of 625 is advanced attainment, 300 is minimum
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: More years in a classroom is not the same as more learning; on harmonised tests an Indian child's measured learning trails Vietnam's and East Asia's by a wide margin.

plannedCharts.title: Where are the women at work?
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank / ILO modelled estimate · share of women 15+ in the labour force
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: India's single most striking outlier: barely a quarter to a third of women are in the measured workforce, far below its Asian peers.

plannedCharts.title: How fast families shrank
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank · total fertility rate · 1960 to latest
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Faster fertility decline opened the demographic-dividend window earlier in East Asia.

plannedCharts.title: Children too short for their age
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank · child stunting, latest available year per country
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Stunting is malnutrition written into a child's body and brain; India's rate is high even against much poorer countries.

plannedCharts.title: How much each country built
plannedCharts.unit: gross fixed capital formation (% of GDP)
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank · gross fixed capital formation as a share of GDP · the investment rate
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The under-told engine of the miracle: East Asia poured a huge share of output into factories, roads and machines.

plannedCharts.title: Who saved to pay for it
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank · gross savings as a share of GDP
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: High investment was financed by high domestic saving; the two move together.

plannedCharts.title: Foreign money coming in
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank · foreign direct investment, net inflows, as a share of GDP
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Foreign factories brought capital, technology and export markets; Vietnam and China pulled in far more, relative to their size.

plannedCharts.title: How deep the banks went
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank · domestic credit to the private sector as a share of GDP · how much finance reaches firms and households
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Investment needs finance; East Asia's banks pushed far more credit into private hands, while India's financial system stayed shallow for decades.

plannedCharts.title: What each worker has to work with
plannedCharts.subtitle: Penn World Table 10.01 · capital stock per worker · the machines, buildings and infrastructure behind each job
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Decades of higher investment compound into the tools each worker has; an Indian worker today has a small fraction of the capital a Korean worker does.

plannedCharts.title: The factory escalator India never rode
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank · manufacturing value added as a share of GDP · India and South Korea have full records; China's WB series starts only in 2004
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Manufacturing is the escalator out of poverty; Korea's share humped up and stayed, India's never really rose.

plannedCharts.title: India's leap from farm to office
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank · India's value added by sector · the structural leap that skipped the factory
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: India's workers and output moved from farms to services, largely skipping the mass-manufacturing stage in between.

plannedCharts.title: Who left the farm, and when
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank / ILO modelled estimate · share of workers in agriculture
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Development means moving workers off the farm into higher-productivity work; India did this slower than its peers.

plannedCharts.title: The kind of work India made: informal
plannedCharts.subtitle: ILOSTAT · share of employment that is informal · jobs without contracts, social security or stable pay
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The factory job is a formal job with a payslip; the work India created instead was overwhelmingly informal, around nine in ten jobs without contract or security.

plannedCharts.title: The tariff wall India kept up
plannedCharts.subtitle: WITS · effectively-applied tariff, simple average across all products (after trade deals and exemptions) · how walled-off each market stayed
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Export-led growth needs an open economy; even after decades of liberalisation India still levies the highest effective tariff of the group.

plannedCharts.title: India's wall, and how much it waives
plannedCharts.subtitle: WITS · India's most-favoured-nation tariff versus its effectively-applied tariff · the gap is the discount given through trade deals and exemptions
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: India's headline tariff overstates its openness: a meaningful slice is waived through preferential deals, but the effective wall is still the group's tallest.

plannedCharts.title: Climbing the complexity ladder
plannedCharts.subtitle: Harvard Growth Lab Atlas of Economic Complexity · how diverse and sophisticated each country's exports are
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: It is not just how much you export but what: Korea and China climbed to complex, high-value goods while India's basket stayed simpler.

plannedCharts.title: Making things to sell the world
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank · manufactured goods as a share of merchandise exports
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Export-led growth runs on selling manufactures to the world; the peers built that engine, India leaned more on services and commodities.

plannedCharts.title: Who captured world trade
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank / WTO · each country's goods exports as a share of all world goods exports
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The clearest single picture of the divergence in trade: China's share of world exports went from around 1% to over 14%, while India's barely moved off 1-2%.

plannedCharts.title: Plugged into the world's supply chains
plannedCharts.subtitle: OECD TiVA 2025 · foreign value added as a share of gross exports · how plugged-in each country is to global supply chains (backward GVC participation)
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Modern manufacturing means importing parts, adding value and re-exporting; Vietnam wove itself deep into these chains, India far less so.

plannedCharts.title: Becoming China's customer
plannedCharts.subtitle: UN Comtrade · India's imports from and exports to China · the trade relationship that ran one way
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: As China became the world's factory, India became one of its customers: imports from China exploded while India's exports back stayed flat, a widening deficit.

plannedCharts.title: How much each worker produces
plannedCharts.subtitle: Penn World Table via Our World in Data · real GDP per hour worked
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The income gap is, at bottom, a productivity gap: how much value an hour of work creates.

plannedCharts.title: Spending on inventing the future
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank · gross domestic expenditure on research and development as a share of GDP
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Korea now spends a world-leading share on R&D; India's has been stuck below one percent for decades.

plannedCharts.title: The power to run a factory
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank · electric power consumption per person · a proxy for industrial and household capacity
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Power per person tracks how industrial and how comfortable a society has become.

plannedCharts.title: Moving to the city
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank · share of population living in urban areas
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Factories and services cluster in cities; East Asia urbanised fast, India more slowly and messily.

plannedCharts.title: The capable state
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators · government effectiveness, ranked against all countries · the state's capacity to deliver
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Behind the policy choices sits the machine that carries them out; East Asia built states that could plan, target and deliver, and India's measured effectiveness has stayed middling.

plannedCharts.title: Where India scores, and where it doesn't
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators · India's latest percentile rank on each of the six dimensions · India is not uniformly weak
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: India's institutional story is not a flat failure: it ranks respectably on voice and the rule of law, and far lower on the capacity to regulate, deliver and curb corruption.

plannedCharts.title: The growth-rate gap behind the income gap
plannedCharts.unit: real GDP per capita growth (% per year, decade average)
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank / Maddison · average annual growth of GDP per capita, by decade · small gaps compound into the income chasm
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The income gap is compound interest: East Asia grew its income per head 6-9% a year for decades while India managed 1-2% before 1980, and a few points a year, sustained, becomes everything.

plannedCharts.title: Sweat or smarts?
plannedCharts.subtitle: Penn World Table 10.01 · total factor productivity relative to the United States · efficiency, after counting labour and capital
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Was the miracle just piling up capital and labour, or using them better? Korea and Taiwan raised efficiency toward the US frontier; India's gain has been slow.

plannedCharts.title: The demographic window, and who used it
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank · share of the population of working age · the dividend window opens when this rises
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: A rising working-age share is a tailwind, but only if those workers find productive jobs; East Asia turned its window into factory work, India's is open now.

plannedCharts.title: Did the growth reach everyone?
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Inequality Database · share of pre-tax national income going to the top 10% · who captured the gains
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Growth and fairness are not the same question; India's top tenth now takes a larger slice of income than in almost any major economy, a sharper rise than its East Asian peers.

plannedCharts.title: So when does India catch up?
plannedCharts.unit: GDP per capita at PPP (constant 2021 int-$)
plannedCharts.subtitle: Indica projection · India's income per person extended at its recent real growth rate, against where China and South Korea stand today
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: If India keeps growing at its recent pace, it reaches China's current income level only around 2043, and is still short of Korea's by mid-century, a sobering read on how long the gap takes to close.

plannedCharts.title: The poverty India did crush
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank Poverty and Inequality Platform via Our World in Data · share below the $3-a-day extreme-poverty line
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: India's genuine win: hundreds of millions lifted out of extreme poverty, even without the manufacturing boom.

plannedCharts.title: India's other escalator: services
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank balance-of-payments data · services as a share of goods-plus-services exports · India's distinctive tilt toward selling services, not goods
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: India did build an export engine, but in services (IT, business services) rather than factory goods, a different escalator that lifts fewer low-skilled workers.

plannedCharts.title: The all-in human scorecard
plannedCharts.subtitle: UNDP via Our World in Data · Human Development Index, combining health, schooling and income
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: A single composite of health, schooling and income, to see the whole gap at once.

plannedCharts.title: The road not taken: democracy
plannedCharts.subtitle: V-Dem via Our World in Data · electoral democracy index · India stayed democratic; Korea and Taiwan democratised only after their growth takeoff
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The honest counterweight: India built its record under continuous democracy, while the East Asian transformations were often coerced and only democratised later.

plannedCharts.title: What India's firms say holds them back
plannedCharts.subtitle: World Bank Enterprise Survey, India 2014 · share of firms naming each as their single biggest obstacle · one dated snapshot, read as texture not trend
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: From the businesses' own mouths: a decade ago Indian firms ranked corruption and unreliable electricity, not labour laws, as their biggest obstacles, a useful corrective to easy assumptions about what holds growth back.
